newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine car market growing, price wars likely.
newsitem.headline: Philippine car market growing, price wars likely.

text.p: Philippine car sales are expected to remain buoyant in 1997 as the economy grows, but intense competition and price wars could drive some manufacturers out of the market, industry officials said this week.
Ever since the government opened the car industry to more players in 1990, the number of assembly plants in the country has grown to 11 from three.

Those already present -- Toyota Motor Corp, Mitsubishi Motors Corp and Nissan Motor Co Ltd -- had been joined by other top Japanese, European and South Korean car makers and Ford Motor Co was looking to set up assembly facilities in the Philippines, industry sources said.
The fight for market share erupted into slashes in car prices by as much as 30 percent during Christmas promotions this year. It also encouraged an array of liberal financing schemes.

"If this pricing war continues, only big manufacturers can survive and the small manufacturers who cannot afford to compete will have to go," said Koji Miyajima, president of Honda Motor's unit, Honda Cars Philippines Inc.
"It seems the whole year round there were discounts. The competition was really very tight," said Florencio Jurado, senior vice-president of Toyota Motor Philippines Corp.
He said he would not be surprised if some players backed out.
Honda and Toyota currently account for the biggest shares in the market at 23 and 22 percent respectively.
But Peter Garrucho, president of the Chamber of Automotive Manufacturers of the Philippines Inc, said there was room for the market to grow.
"There's a long way to go as long as the economy is growing," he said. "Many (manufacturers) are still expecting growing sales but they're sacrificing margins."
A survey by a leading car maker of nine manufacturers showed a return on sales of 6.0 percent to a negative 3.7 percent on various models in 1995.

Others said the continuing lack of mass transit systems in Manila and other major cities made the purchase of a car a necessity for middle-class Filipinos. The demand for taxis was also rising, they said.

Garrucho, however, said car assemblers had adopted a conservative stance on their sales projections next year. "Most companies are projecting about 10 percent growth. Companies tend to be more cautious because of the competition," he said.
Nevertheless, he said car sales in the first 11 months this year jumped by 24 percent to 80,503 units from 64,744 in the same 1995 period.
The industry had grown by a yearly average of 26 percent in the last five years as the economy has expanded, he added.
Honda's Miyajima said car sales in the Philippines could grow by 18 to 20 percent in 1997 to more than 100,000 units.

Honda itself sees a 15 percent increase in sales in 1997 to at least 23,000 units after a huge 80 percent growth this year. Honda, however, had not joined the race to slash prices, relying more on quality and after-sales service, Miyajima said.
"We are enjoying good sales this year even without discounts," he said.
Honda and Toyota have also said they will continue to expand their operations in the Philippines.

Toyota will complete a 2.5 billion-peso investment in a new plant early next year that will raise its annual capacity by 25,000 to 65,000 units, while Honda spent 270 million pesos early in the year to hike its capacity by 10,000 to 35,000 units.
"We are always competing. We have to be constantly innovating and re-engineering," Jurado said.
